lessons.title: Floyd-Warshall All Pairs Shortest Path
lessons.objective: Implement Floyd-Warshall for all-pairs shortest paths in O(V³), understand the DP recurrence, and detect negative cycles.
concepts: All-pairs shortest path (APSP): shortest path between every pair of vertices
Floyd-Warshall: O(V^3) time, O(V^2) space DP on intermediate vertices
Recurrence: dist[i][j] = min(dist[i][j], dist[i][k] + dist[k][j])
Outer loop: k = intermediate vertex allowed in the path
Initialisation: dist[i][i]=0, dist[i][j]=edge weight, Infinity if no edge
Negative cycle detection: if dist[i][i] < 0 after all iterations
Handles negative weights (but not negative cycles)
Path reconstruction: track predecessor matrix
lessons.explanation: Floyd-Warshall computes shortest paths between all pairs of vertices. The DP recurrence: dist[i][j][k] = minimum path from i to j using only vertices {0, 1, ..., k} as intermediates. After processing all k intermediate vertices, dist[i][j] is the true shortest path. The outer loop iterates k from 0 to V-1. The transition: for each pair (i, j), check if routing through k gives a shorter path: dist[i][j] = min(dist[i][j], dist[i][k] + dist[k][j]). Initialise: dist[i][i] = 0, dist[i][j] = edge weight if edge exists, else Infinity. Negative cycle detection: if dist[i][i] < 0 for any i after all iterations, there is a negative cycle reachable from i. Difference from running Dijkstra V times: Floyd-Warshall handles negative weights and is simpler for dense graphs. For sparse graphs, running Dijkstra V times (O(V * (V+E) log V)) is faster when E << V².
lessons.analogy: Floyd-Warshall is like discovering shortcuts in a city by progressively considering more intermediate stops. Round 1: can going through city 0 shorten any direct route? Round 2: can going through cities 0 or 1 shorten any route? After V rounds: can any of the V cities serve as a shortcut? Each round potentially improves all paths simultaneously.

code_example.explanation: The outer loop order (k before i before j) is critical. k must be the outermost loop because when processing intermediate vertex k, all shortest paths using only vertices 0 through k-1 must already be computed (in dist[i][k] and dist[k][j]). If k were not the outermost loop, these values would be partially updated and the recurrence would be incorrect.

common_mistakes: Not putting k as the outermost loop — k must be outermost so that dist[i][k] and dist[k][j] are the shortest paths through vertices {0..k-1} when computing paths through k; incorrect ordering produces wrong distances
Not initialising the diagonal to 0 — dist[i][i] should be 0 (zero cost to stay at i); without this, paths through i as intermediate will not be computed correctly
Not detecting negative cycles — after the DP, check if any dist[i][i] < 0; if so, a negative cycle exists and shortest paths are undefined for vertices reachable from/through the cycle
lessons.interview_relevance: Floyd-Warshall is NeetCode 150 via Find the City With Smallest Number of Neighbors (#1334). It is the standard all-pairs shortest path algorithm and appears when problems require distances between all pairs of vertices. The comparison with running Dijkstra V times (O(V*(V+E) log V)) is specifically asked: 'When would you choose Floyd-Warshall over Dijkstra?'
lessons.mini_challenge: Implement floydWarshall and verify result[0][2]=4 and result[0][3]=5 for the test graph. Implement findTheCity and verify it returns 3. Then solve Find the City (#1334) on your own without looking at the solution. Finally, construct a 4-node graph with a negative cycle and verify that floydWarshall returns null. Which node will have dist[i][i] < 0?

flashcards.front: Floyd-Warshall: what does it compute?
flashcards.back: ALL-PAIRS SHORTEST PATHS: the shortest path between every pair of vertices (u, v) simultaneously. O(V³) time, O(V²) space. Works with negative edge weights (but not negative cycles). The only algorithm to solve all-pairs in one pass.

flashcards.front: Floyd-Warshall recurrence?
flashcards.back: dist[i][j] = min(dist[i][j], dist[i][k] + dist[k][j]) for each intermediate vertex k. The outer loop is over k (possible intermediate vertices), then i and j. Semantics: is going through k a shorter path from i to j?

flashcards.front: Floyd-Warshall: initialisation?
flashcards.back: dist[i][i] = 0. dist[i][j] = weight of edge (i,j) if it exists. dist[i][j] = Infinity if no direct edge. Then apply the triple loop. After the algorithm, dist[i][j] = shortest path from i to j.

flashcards.front: Floyd-Warshall: negative cycle detection?
flashcards.back: After the algorithm, if dist[i][i] < 0 for any i: a negative cycle is reachable from (and back to) i. The main diagonal should remain 0 for graphs without negative cycles.

flashcards.front: Floyd-Warshall: path reconstruction?
flashcards.back: Maintain a 'next' matrix. next[i][j] = j initially (direct edge). When dist[i][k]+dist[k][j] < dist[i][j]: next[i][j] = next[i][k]. To reconstruct path i→j: follow next[i][j] until reaching j.

flashcards.front: Floyd-Warshall vs V×Dijkstra: when is Floyd-Warshall preferred?
flashcards.back: Dense graphs (E ≈ V²): Floyd O(V³) vs Dijkstra O(V × (V+E) log V) ≈ O(V³ log V) — Floyd wins slightly. Negative edges present: Dijkstra fails, Floyd handles them. Small V (≤ 500): Floyd's simplicity wins. Large sparse graphs: V×Dijkstra is better.

quiz.question: Floyd-Warshall on 3 vertices, edges: 0→1(4), 0→2(11), 1→2(2). After k=1: dist[0][2] = ?
options: 6 (via vertex 1: 4+2=6)
11 (direct)
quiz.explanation: k=1 (vertex 1 as intermediate): dist[0][2] = min(dist[0][2], dist[0][1]+dist[1][2]) = min(11, 4+2) = 6. Going 0→1→2 costs 6, better than direct 0→2 which costs 11.

quiz.question: Floyd-Warshall detects negative cycles when?
options: Any edge has negative weight
dist[i][j] < 0 for some i ≠ j
dist[i][i] < 0 for some i (diagonal becomes negative)
The algorithm doesn't terminate
quiz.explanation: Initially dist[i][i]=0. If a negative cycle includes vertex i, after the algorithm dist[i][i] < 0 (the cycle can be traversed to improve the i→i path). Check all diagonal entries after the algorithm.

quiz.question: For 4 vertices, how many iterations does Floyd-Warshall perform?
quiz.explanation: Triple nested loop: k from 0 to V-1, i from 0 to V-1, j from 0 to V-1. V³ = 4³ = 64 iterations.

quiz.question: Floyd-Warshall: the outer loop is over k (intermediate vertex). Why must k be the OUTERMOST loop?
options: Convention only — any loop order works

For correctness: dist[i][k][j] at iteration k means paths using only vertices 0..k as intermediates. If k were inner, we'd use k as intermediate before computing paths through smaller-indexed intermediates.
To optimize cache performance
k must be outermost to handle negative edges
quiz.explanation: The algorithm's invariant: after processing k, dist[i][j] = shortest path from i to j using only vertices {0,1,...,k} as intermediates. This invariant requires k to increase outermost. If i or j were outermost, we'd use larger k values before smaller ones, breaking the invariant.

complexity_summary.vs_v_dijkstra: Floyd simpler for dense graphs or when negative edges present; V×Dijkstra for sparse non-negative graphs

theory_mcq.question: In Floyd-Warshall, the outer loop iterates over INTERMEDIATE vertex k, and the inner loops iterate over source i and destination j. Why must k be the OUTERMOST loop?
options: k as the outer loop is an arbitrary convention; any order works

CORRECTNESS REQUIRES k OUTERMOST: the recurrence `dist[i][j] = min(dist[i][j], dist[i][k]+dist[k][j])` means 'shortest path from i to j using only vertices 0..k as intermediates'; when we compute dist[i][j] for a given k, we rely on dist[i][k] and dist[k][j] being ALREADY FULLY COMPUTED for all intermediate vertices 0..k-1; if k were inner, dist[i][k] might not yet reflect paths through intermediate vertices 0..k-1, giving wrong results; k outermost guarantees the DP builds up the path set incrementally and correctly
k outermost gives O(V³); k innermost would be O(V⁴)
k outermost prevents negative cycle detection from triggering prematurely
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's concept: 'Outer loop: k = intermediate vertex allowed in the path' — the DP invariant: after iteration k, dist[i][j] = shortest path from i to j using ONLY vertices {0,...,k} as intermediates; this invariant requires that when computing round k, paths through {0,...,k-1} are already optimal (from prior rounds); k as the outermost loop enforces this ordering.

theory_mcq.question: Floyd-Warshall detects negative cycles by checking `dist[i][i] < 0` AFTER all iterations. Why does a negative diagonal entry indicate a negative cycle?
options: dist[i][i] < 0 means vertex i has a negative self-loop

dist[i][i] represents the SHORTEST CYCLE THROUGH VERTEX i; initially dist[i][i]=0 (no movement); after Floyd-Warshall, dist[i][i] < 0 means the algorithm found a PATH from i back to i with NEGATIVE TOTAL WEIGHT — a negative cycle; any vertex on this negative cycle will have its own dist[i][i] updated to negative; this is the canonical Floyd-Warshall negative cycle check; if a negative cycle exists and vertex i is ON that cycle, the path i→(cycle)→i has negative total weight
dist[i][i] < 0 indicates a disconnected graph
Negative diagonal only appears when there are exactly two negative edges
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's concept: 'Negative cycle detection: if dist[i][i] < 0 after all iterations' — dist[i][i]=0 initially (cost of staying in place); if after running Floyd-Warshall dist[i][i] < 0, the algorithm found a path from i back to i through intermediate vertices that has negative total weight — this is exactly a negative cycle containing i.

dist[0][3]=7: path 0->1->2->3=3+INF=impossible; path 0->1->3=3+4=7

Other cities reach more. City 3 wins (and has largest index among tied).
City 0: reaches all cities within distance 4 (via 0-1-2-3=5 edges, too far for city 3)
City 2: reaches only city 1 within distance 4

syntax_mcq.question: In Floyd-Warshall, `const dist = graph.map(row => [...row])` creates a DEEP COPY (one level). Why is this necessary?
options: The copy is optional; modifying the original graph is acceptable

WITHOUT COPYING: the algorithm modifies dist[i][j] in place during iterations; if dist is the original graph, we'd be corrupting the input data; more critically, for a row matrix `dist[i][j]` might later be used to derive other values in the same outer-k iteration — modifying it in place could use the ALREADY-UPDATED dist[i][j] as if it were the original, causing incorrect DP computation; the spread operator `[...row]` creates a SHALLOW COPY of each row (sufficient since rows contain numbers, not objects)
The copy is needed to avoid aliasing of row arrays in JavaScript
graph.map always modifies the original array, so a copy is mandatory
syntax_mcq.explanation: The shallow copy (`[...row]`) is necessary because: (1) preserves the input graph, (2) the DP correctly reads original values; since matrix cells are numbers (primitives), a one-level spread is a sufficient deep copy; `graph.map(row=>[...row])` creates new array objects for each row while copying primitive values — exactly what's needed for an independent dist matrix.

lessons.title: Tarjan's SCC Algorithm
lessons.objective: Implement Tarjan's algorithm to find strongly connected components in O(V+E) using a DFS stack and low-link values, and understand why the low-link value enables SCC detection.
concepts: SCC: maximal set of vertices where every vertex is reachable from every other
Tarjan's uses DFS order and a stack
disc[v]: DFS discovery time of v
low[v]: minimum disc reachable from the subtree rooted at v
Stack: vertices currently in the DFS path that may belong to current SCC
SCC root: vertex where low[v] == disc[v] (no back-edge to earlier vertex)
Pop the stack when SCC root is found: all vertices above = one SCC
O(V+E): each vertex and edge processed once
lessons.explanation: Strongly Connected Components (SCCs) are maximal subgraphs where every pair of vertices can reach each other. Tarjan's algorithm finds all SCCs in O(V+E) using a single DFS. Each vertex gets a discovery time disc[v] (DFS order) and a low-link value low[v] (minimum disc reachable via back edges from v's subtree). A vertex v is the root of an SCC if low[v] == disc[v] (no back edge reaches an earlier vertex, meaning nothing in v's subtree can escape to an earlier part of the DFS tree). When such a root is found, pop all vertices from the stack down to and including v — they form one SCC. The stack contains vertices that are in the current DFS path and have not yet been assigned to an SCC. The key update rule: after recursing into a child u, update low[v] = min(low[v], low[u]). For a back edge to an already-visited vertex u that is still on the stack, update low[v] = min(low[v], disc[u]).
lessons.analogy: Tarjan's algorithm is like finding islands in a network of one-way roads. You drive through the network in DFS order. A vertex is an 'island exit' (SCC root) if no road from its territory leads back to an earlier-discovered territory. When you find an exit, you claim all the territory you've been driving through since entering (everything on the stack above the exit) as one island (SCC).

code_example.explanation: The onStack check (for back edges) is crucial. When visiting a neighbour u that has already been discovered (disc[u] != -1), only update low[v] if u is still on the stack (onStack[u] is true). If u is not on the stack, it has already been assigned to a different SCC and its low-link information should not propagate back — u's SCC is 'completed' and crossing into it is not a back edge within the current SCC.

common_mistakes: Using disc[u] instead of low[u] when updating low[v] after a tree edge — for tree edges (recursion), propagate low[u] (which may include back edges from u's subtree); for back edges, use disc[u] (the discovery time of the reached vertex)

Not using the onStack check for back edges — if u has been fully processed (not on stack), it belongs to a different SCC; using low[u] instead of disc[u] for such 'cross edges' would incorrectly merge SCCs
Not handling disconnected components — the outer loop must start DFS from every unvisited vertex; a single DFS from vertex 0 misses components not reachable from 0
lessons.interview_relevance: Tarjan's SCC appears in network analysis problems at infrastructure-focused companies (finding strongly connected clusters in dependency graphs, detecting circular dependencies in build systems). Critical Connections in a Network (#1192, NeetCode 150) uses a related technique (bridge-finding DFS). Understanding low-link values is the shared foundation.

flashcards.front: Tarjan's SCC: what is a Strongly Connected Component?
flashcards.back: A maximal set of vertices where every vertex is reachable from every other vertex via directed edges. In an SCC, for every pair (u, v): u→v AND v→u (direct or through paths). A single vertex with no self-loop is a trivial SCC.

flashcards.front: Tarjan's SCC: two key arrays?
flashcards.back: disc[v]: DFS discovery time (timestamp when v is first visited). low[v]: the lowest disc value reachable from v's subtree via back edges or cross edges to ancestors. If low[v] == disc[v]: v is the ROOT of an SCC.

flashcards.front: Tarjan's SCC: low[v] update rules?
flashcards.back: For each neighbor u: if unvisited → recurse, then low[v] = min(low[v], low[u]). If visited AND u is on the DFS stack → low[v] = min(low[v], disc[u]). The stack membership check is critical: visited BUT NOT on stack means u is in an already-completed SCC.

flashcards.front: Tarjan's SCC: when is a vertex the SCC root?
flashcards.back: When low[v] == disc[v] after processing all neighbours. This means v cannot reach any ancestor of v through back edges. v is the 'topmost' vertex in its SCC. Pop the stack until v is popped — all popped vertices form the SCC.

flashcards.front: Tarjan's SCC: time complexity and what it produces?
flashcards.back: O(V + E) — each vertex and edge processed once. Produces all SCCs in TOPOLOGICAL ORDER of the condensation DAG (SCCs appear in reverse topological order of the original graph).

flashcards.front: SCC condensation DAG: what is it?
flashcards.back: Contract each SCC to a single node. The resulting graph of SCCs is always a DAG (no cycles — if there were a cycle of SCCs, they'd form one larger SCC). Topological sort on this DAG answers questions like 'is vertex u reachable from vertex v?'

quiz.question: Graph: 1→2→3→1 (triangle), 3→4. SCCs are?
quiz.explanation: 1→2→3→1: all three are mutually reachable (1→2→3→1→...). SCC = {1,2,3}. Vertex 4: reachable from 3 but no path back to 3 (4 has no outgoing edges to {1,2,3}). SCC = {4}.

quiz.question: Tarjan's: vertex v has disc[v]=3, low[v]=3 after DFS completes. What does this mean?
options: v can reach vertex with disc=3
v is the root of an SCC — pop stack until v to get the SCC
v has a self-loop
v was visited at time 3
quiz.explanation: low[v] == disc[v] = 3: the lowest ancestor v can reach (through the subtree) is v itself. No back edge reaches above v. v is an SCC root. Pop the DFS stack until v is removed — all those vertices form one SCC.

quiz.question: Tarjan's: why check 'u is on DFS stack' before updating low[v] = min(low[v], disc[u])?
options: Stack membership is faster to check than disc values
If u is NOT on stack, u is in an already-completed SCC — using disc[u] would incorrectly merge separate SCCs
On-stack check prevents negative disc values
No reason — can always update with disc[u]
quiz.explanation: If u was visited but not on the DFS stack, u has already been assigned to a completed SCC. Using disc[u] to update low[v] would suggest v can reach u's ancestor — but that ancestor is in a different (completed) SCC. This would incorrectly merge v's SCC with u's completed SCC.

quiz.question: For a DAG (no cycles), what is each vertex's SCC?
options: The entire DAG is one SCC
Each vertex is its own trivial SCC (size 1)
SCCs = connected components of the underlying undirected graph
SCCs = topological levels
quiz.explanation: In a DAG, no vertex can reach any of its ancestors (no cycles by definition). Therefore every vertex is trivially its own SCC. Tarjan's on a DAG returns n SCCs, each containing exactly one vertex.

complexity_summary.output_order: SCCs appear in reverse topological order of condensation DAG
complexity_summary.vs_kosaraju: Both O(V+E); Tarjan needs 1 DFS, Kosaraju needs 2. Tarjan is standard in competitive programming.

theory_mcq.question: In Tarjan's SCC, why is `low[v]` defined as the minimum `disc` reachable from the subtree of v (not the minimum `low` of all reachable vertices)?
options: low[v] is the minimum disc of all vertices reachable from v via any path

low[v] specifically tracks vertices reachable via BACK EDGES IN THE DFS TREE from within the subtree: (1) disc[v] itself, (2) disc of vertices reachable via back edges from v's subtree (NOT through cross edges to vertices already finalized in their own SCCs); when a cross edge (v→u) exists where disc[u]!=-1 but u is NOT on the stack (already in another SCC), that SCC is separate — low[v] should NOT inherit low[u]; restricting to onStack vertices ensures low correctly identifies if v's subtree can 'escape' to an earlier DFS ancestor in the SAME potential SCC
low[v] equals low of the direct parent to simplify propagation
low[v] is defined as the minimum vertex index for alphabetical ordering
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's code: `else if(onStack[u]) low[v]=Math.min(low[v],disc[u])` — only back edges to vertices on the stack (in the current DFS path/potential SCC) update low[v]; cross edges to vertices already assigned to finalized SCCs are ignored; this ensures low[v] only reflects connections within the current SCC being discovered.

theory_mcq.question: When Tarjan's finds an SCC root (low[v] == disc[v]), it pops ALL vertices above v from the stack. Why does the stack contain exactly the current SCC's vertices?
options: The stack contains vertices in random order; only popping to v is correct

The STACK MAINTAINS DFS PATH vertices not yet assigned to an SCC: when we push v, it starts a new potential SCC; vertices pushed AFTER v (deeper in DFS) can only reach ancestors via back edges to disc[ancestor] >= disc[v] (since v is the root of this SCC); all vertices between v and the stack top are in the subtree of v's SCC — they can reach v but not any vertex with disc < disc[v] (otherwise low[v] < disc[v] and v wouldn't be an SCC root); popping until v collects exactly the current SCC
The stack contains only leaf vertices; internal nodes are handled separately
Popping to v is an approximation; some vertices may be incorrectly included
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's concept: 'SCC root: vertex where low[v] == disc[v] (no back-edge to earlier vertex)' — if low[v]==disc[v], no vertex in v's subtree can reach any vertex with disc < disc[v]; therefore all vertices between v and the stack top belong to the same SCC; they're bounded between disc[v] and the current DFS time — exactly v's SCC.

logic_mcq.question: For the graph edges [[0,1],[1,2],[2,0],[1,3],[3,4],[4,3]], Tarjan's finds 2 SCCs. What are they?
options: SCC1 = {3,4} (cycle 3↔4); SCC2 = {0,1,2} (cycle 0→1→2→0) — confirmed by execution
logic_mcq.explanation: Confirmed by direct execution: tarjanSCC returns 2 SCCs: {3,4} (3→4→3 cycle) and {0,1,2} (0→1→2→0 cycle); vertex 1 has edges to both 2 (in its SCC) and 3 (in a different SCC), but 3 cannot reach 1, so 3 is in a separate SCC.

logic_mcq.question: Why does Tarjan's need the `onStack` boolean array in ADDITION to `disc` (which tracks if a vertex was visited)?
options: onStack is redundant; disc!=-1 already captures the same information

disc[u] != -1 means u WAS VISITED but doesn't tell us if u is CURRENTLY ON THE STACK; a vertex is removed from the stack when its SCC is finalised; if v has an edge to u where disc[u]!=-1 and onStack[u]=false, u already belongs to a COMPLETED SCC — low[v] should NOT be updated (that SCC is separate); if onStack[u]=true, u is still in the current DFS path and belongs to the same potential SCC — low[v] should be updated; without onStack, Tarjan's would incorrectly merge separate SCCs
onStack tracks whether u has been processed in the outer for loop
onStack is needed only for disconnected graphs with multiple components
logic_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's code: `else if(onStack[u]) low[v]=Math.min(low[v],disc[u])` — the distinction: disc[u]!=-1 && onStack[u]=true: u is in the current DFS path, same potential SCC; disc[u]!=-1 && onStack[u]=false: u already finalized in a different SCC; without onStack, cross edges to finalized SCCs would incorrectly lower low[v], merging separate SCCs.

syntax_mcq.question: Tarjan's uses `do { w = stack.pop(); } while (w !== v)` to collect SCC members. Why `do-while` instead of `while`?
options: do-while is required because the stack could be empty when checked

DO-WHILE ensures v ITSELF is always popped (the SCC root): `while (w !== v)` would only pop vertices BEFORE v and stop; since v IS the SCC root and IS on the stack, we need to pop v as well; do-while evaluates the body FIRST, then checks the condition — it always pops at least once (getting v even if v is at the top); using a regular while with `w !== v` as the condition would need to check before popping, complicating the code or missing v
do-while is used for performance; while would be equivalent
The stack invariant ensures at least 2 elements before this code; do-while handles the 2-element case
syntax_mcq.explanation: The do-while pattern: pop first, then check if we've reached v; this ensures v is popped (v is the SCC root and must be included in the SCC); the equivalent while loop would be: `while(true) { w=stack.pop(); scc.push(w); if(w===v) break; }` — functionally identical but less idiomatic; do-while is natural for 'pop at least once' patterns.

lessons.title: Bridges And Articulation Points
lessons.objective: Find all bridges and articulation points in an undirected graph using DFS discovery and low values in O(V+E), detecting edges and vertices whose removal disconnects the graph.
concepts: Bridge: edge whose removal increases the number of connected components
Articulation point: vertex whose removal increases the number of connected components
DFS tree: the edges traversed during DFS form a spanning tree
disc[v]: DFS discovery time of v
low[v]: minimum discovery time reachable from v without using its parent edge
Bridge condition: low[v] > disc[u] for edge u-v (no back edge bypasses this edge)
Articulation point condition: low[v] >= disc[u] for non-root, or root with 2+ children
O(V+E): single DFS pass
lessons.explanation: Bridges and articulation points identify critical infrastructure in an undirected graph. A bridge (u, v) is critical if removing it disconnects the graph — equivalently, there is no back edge from v's subtree that reaches u or an ancestor of u. The DFS-based algorithm: assign each vertex a discovery time disc[v] and a low value low[v] = the minimum discovery time reachable from v's subtree using at most one back edge. Bridge condition: edge (u, v) is a bridge if low[v] > disc[u] (no vertex in v's subtree can reach u or u's ancestors without using this edge). Articulation point condition: vertex u is an articulation point if: (1) u is not the root and some child v has low[v] >= disc[u] (v's subtree cannot bypass u), or (2) u is the root and has 2+ children in the DFS tree (removing root disconnects those subtrees). The update rule for low: low[v] = min(low[v], disc[u]) for back edges to u, and low[v] = min(low[v], low[child]) for tree edges (after recursing).
lessons.analogy: Bridges are like single-lane bridges on a road network: if you remove one, some areas become isolated. Articulation points are like critical intersections: if the intersection is closed, some areas lose all access. The low-link value is a 'bypass check': for each road, does the territory beyond it have an alternate route back to the main network? If not, the road is a bridge and the intersection at its start is an articulation point.

code_example.explanation: The root articulation point check (childCount >= 2) is a special case because the low-link condition low[u] >= disc[v] would always be true for the root (disc[root] = 0, and all discovery times are >= 0). The root is an articulation point only if removing it would separate its children into disconnected groups, which happens exactly when it has 2+ DFS tree children.

common_mistakes: Using low[u] > disc[v] for articulation points instead of low[u] >= disc[v] — bridges use strict > (u's subtree cannot reach v or above); articulation points use >= (u's subtree cannot reach strictly above v, but can reach v itself which won't help if v is removed)

Not handling the root as a special case — the standard low[u] >= disc[v] check incorrectly classifies the root as an articulation point even with one child; check childCount >= 2 separately for the root

Skipping the parent edge in undirected graphs — in undirected graphs, each edge appears twice in the adjacency list; without skipping the parent, every tree edge would become a back edge, corrupting all low values
lessons.interview_relevance: Critical Connections in a Network (#1192) is NeetCode 150 and directly tests bridge-finding. It appears at Facebook/Meta specifically for network reliability questions: 'Find all connections in a network whose failure would disconnect the network.' Articulation points appear in 'Find single points of failure in an infrastructure graph.' Both are O(V+E) DFS problems.

flashcards.front: Bridge in an undirected graph: definition?
flashcards.back: An edge (u, v) is a BRIDGE if removing it increases the number of connected components. Equivalently: (u,v) is a bridge iff there is no back edge that 'bypasses' it (no alternative path from u's subtree to v's ancestors other than through (u,v)).

flashcards.front: Bridge detection: disc/low algorithm?
flashcards.back: During DFS, edge (parent, child): if low[child] > disc[parent]: this edge is a bridge (no back edge from child's subtree reaches parent or above). The condition uses STRICT > (not ≥) because an equal means an alternative path exists back through this node.

flashcards.front: Articulation point: definition?
flashcards.back: A vertex v is an ARTICULATION POINT if removing v (and its edges) increases the number of connected components. Two cases: (1) root of DFS tree with ≥ 2 children. (2) non-root v where some child c has low[c] ≥ disc[v] (no back edge from c's subtree bypasses v).

flashcards.front: Articulation point condition: low[c] ≥ disc[v] vs bridge condition: low[c] > disc[parent]?
flashcards.back: BRIDGE (u,v): low[v] > disc[u] (strictly greater — no alternative route back). ARTICULATION POINT at u: low[v] ≥ disc[u] (greater or equal — even if there's a back edge TO u, u is still an AP if the subtree can't bypass u). The ≥ vs > difference is subtle but critical.

flashcards.front: Two-edge-connected components vs biconnected components?
flashcards.back: Two-edge-connected: remove any single EDGE → stays connected (no bridges). Biconnected: remove any single VERTEX → stays connected (no articulation points). Bridges and APs are the boundaries of these components.

flashcards.front: DFS parent tracking in bridge/AP algorithms: why is it needed?
flashcards.back: In an undirected graph DFS, the edge back to the parent is a 'trivial back edge'. When computing low[v], we should NOT use the parent edge to update low[v] (that would make every edge look like it can bypass itself). Pass parent as a parameter and skip the parent when iterating neighbors.

quiz.question: Graph: path 1-2-3-4 (linear chain, undirected). How many bridges?
quiz.explanation: All edges in a tree/path are bridges (no alternative routes). Edges (1,2), (2,3), (3,4): all 3 are bridges. Removing any one disconnects the graph.

quiz.question: Graph: 1-2, 2-3, 3-1 (triangle) plus edge 3-4. Articulation points?
options: None — the triangle protects vertices 1,2,3
Vertex 3 only (removing 3 disconnects 4)
Vertices 1 and 2
Vertex 4
quiz.explanation: Triangle 1-2-3: removing any of 1,2,3 within the triangle still connects the others. But removing 3: vertex 4 becomes disconnected. Only vertex 3 is an AP. AP condition: child(4) has low[4]=disc[4] (no back edge from 4's subtree) ≥ disc[3]. Yes.

quiz.question: Bridge detection: why low[child] > disc[parent] (strict >) but AP detection uses ≥?
options: Arbitrary convention

For bridge (u,v): if low[v]=disc[u], there's a back edge TO u — the edge (u,v) can be bypassed through another path that includes u. For AP: even if low[v]=disc[u] (back edge reaches u), removing u still disconnects v's subtree from u's ancestors above.
Bridge uses strict > because edges are directed
No difference — both use strict >
quiz.explanation: Bridge (u,v): low[v] > disc[u] means v's subtree can't reach u or above → removing edge (u,v) disconnects. If low[v] = disc[u]: back edge reaches exactly u → still connected via that back edge → NOT a bridge. AP at u: even if v's subtree reaches u (low[v]=disc[u]), removing u itself eliminates that connection → IS an AP.

quiz.question: DFS on undirected graph: when tracking parent, what specific scenario does 'skip parent' prevent?
options: Infinite recursion
Incorrectly treating the parent-to-child edge as a back edge and updating low[child] = disc[parent] — making every tree edge look like a bypass
Stack overflow
Visiting the parent node twice
quiz.explanation: In undirected DFS, edge (parent, child) appears as both parent→child (tree edge) and child→parent (neighbor of child). If child uses child→parent to update low[child] = disc[parent], then low[child] ≤ disc[parent] always — making every edge look like it has a bypass. Skipping the parent prevents this false back-edge.

theory_mcq.question: The BRIDGE condition is `low[u] > disc[v]` for tree edge v→u. Why STRICTLY GREATER THAN (not >=)?
options: Strictly greater is used for efficiency; >= would also work

low[u] > disc[v] means: the deepest ancestor reachable from u's ENTIRE SUBTREE has a disc TIME STRICTLY LATER THAN v; i.e., no vertex in u's subtree can reach v OR any ancestor of v via a back edge; removing edge v-u would disconnect u's subtree; low[u] == disc[v] means u's subtree CAN REACH v (via some back edge), so removing v-u doesn't disconnect anything (there's another path to v); strictly greater than disc[v] is the correct bridge condition, >= would miss some bridges (treating edges that go exactly back to v as bridges when they're not)
Strictly greater prevents bridges from being double-counted
>= disc[v] is the correct condition; > is a simplification
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's code: `if(low[u]>disc[v]) bridges.push([v,u])` — if low[u]==disc[v], u's subtree has a back edge reaching v, meaning there's an alternative cycle through v; removing edge v-u doesn't disconnect u's subtree from v (the back edge provides connectivity); only when low[u] > disc[v] (can't reach v or any earlier) does removing v-u disconnect the graph.

theory_mcq.question: The ARTICULATION POINT condition uses `low[u] >= disc[v]` (not strictly greater like bridges). Why >= for APs but > for bridges?
options: Both conditions should use the same operator; the difference is a bug

ARTICULATION POINT >= because: if low[u] == disc[v], u's subtree has a back edge only reaching v itself; removing vertex v would remove THIS back edge too (since v is deleted, not just the edge); u's subtree would be disconnected from v's ancestors; so v IS an articulation point even when low[u]==disc[v]; BRIDGE > because: removing just the EDGE v-u still leaves v in the graph; if u has a back edge to v (low[u]==disc[v]), u can still reach v through this back edge — NOT a bridge; the vertex/edge removal distinction creates this asymmetry
>= is used for AP because the root node requires special handling
The difference is only relevant for multigraphs with parallel edges
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's concepts: 'Articulation point condition: low[v] >= disc[u]' vs 'Bridge condition: low[v] > disc[u]' — removing a VERTEX removes all its incident edges; if u can only reach v (low[u]==disc[v]), removing v severs that connection (AP condition); but removing just the EDGE v-u: if u can reach v via another back edge (low[u]==disc[v]), the graph stays connected (not a bridge); hence strictly greater for bridges.

options: Edge 0-1 is a bridge because node 0 has degree 1 (only connected to node 1); removing it disconnects {0} from the rest of the graph

Edge 0-1 is a bridge because low[1]>disc[0]: the DFS tree has 0 as root with child 1; 1's subtree (nodes 1,2,3,4) has no back edge reaching 0 (no vertex can reach back to 0 since 0 only has the edge to 1); therefore low[1]>disc[0] and removing 0-1 disconnects {0} from {1,2,3,4}
Edge 0-1 is a bridge because node 1 is an articulation point
Edge 0-1 is a bridge because both endpoints have different degrees

options: [[1,3]] because edges 0-1, 1-2, 2-0 form a cycle, so none of them are bridges; only 1-3 (connecting node 3 which has no other connections) is a bridge
[[1,3]] because node 3 has the highest degree
[[1,3]] and [[0,1]] are both bridges; only one is returned
The entire graph minus edge 1-3 is still connected

syntax_mcq.question: The DFS uses `if (u === parent) continue` to skip the parent edge. What problem would occur WITHOUT this check?
options: Without the check, the DFS would revisit the parent correctly via back edge logic

WITHOUT the check: when processing node v's neighbors, the edge back to v's parent p would be seen as a BACK EDGE (since disc[p]!=-1 and p is on the stack); `low[v]=Math.min(low[v],disc[p])` would update low[v] to disc[p]; this means every vertex incorrectly thinks it can reach its parent via a 'back edge'; consequently low[u] == disc[v] for every tree edge v-u (since u sees the edge back to v and sets low[u]=disc[v]); this would mark NO bridges (bridge condition low[u]>disc[v] never satisfied) and wrong articulation points
Without the check, the DFS would revisit all vertices infinitely
The check is optional for directed graphs but required for undirected
syntax_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's code: `if (u === parent) continue` — in undirected graphs, each edge appears in BOTH directions in the adjacency list; when DFS visits v from parent p, adj[v] contains p; without skipping, the parent edge would be treated as a back edge to p, artificially lowering low[v] to disc[p] and eliminating valid bridges; the parent skip is essential for correctness in undirected bridge/AP finding.

lessons.title: Bipartite Graph Matching
lessons.objective: Model bipartite matching as a flow problem, implement augmenting-path maximum matching in O(VE), and understand the connection to max-flow min-cut theorem.
concepts: Bipartite graph: vertices divided into two sets, edges only between sets
Maximum bipartite matching: maximum number of edges with no shared vertices
Augmenting path: alternating unmatched/matched edges from free to free vertex
Hungarian algorithm: find augmenting path via DFS/BFS, O(VE)
König's theorem: max matching = min vertex cover in bipartite graphs
Reduction to max flow: add source/sink, all capacities 1
O(VE) augmenting path, O(E*sqrt(V)) Hopcroft-Karp
Applications: job assignment, task scheduling, stable matching
lessons.explanation: Bipartite matching assigns pairs from two sets with the maximum number of non-conflicting assignments (no vertex used twice). The augmenting path algorithm: maintain a partial matching. Repeatedly find an augmenting path — an alternating path of unmatched, matched, unmatched, ... edges starting and ending at unmatched vertices. Each augmenting path increases the matching by 1. When no augmenting path exists, the matching is maximum. The algorithm runs DFS/BFS from each unmatched left vertex to find an augmenting path. O(V) augmenting paths each taking O(E) DFS = O(VE) total. The reduction to max flow: add a source connected to all left vertices (capacity 1), and a sink connected from all right vertices (capacity 1). All bipartite edges have capacity 1. The maximum flow equals the maximum matching. König's theorem: in bipartite graphs, the size of the maximum matching equals the size of the minimum vertex cover (the minimum set of vertices touching all edges).
lessons.analogy: Bipartite matching is like pairing students with internships. Each student has a list of acceptable companies. You want to maximise the number of students placed. An augmenting path is a chain of reassignments: student A can take company X, but X is taken by student B, who can alternatively take company Y, which is free. Reassigning B to Y frees X for A, gaining one additional placement.

code_example.explanation: The visited array is reset for each left vertex's DFS attempt. This is critical: without resetting, a 'blocked' right vertex from one augmentation attempt would remain blocked for future attempts. The visited array tracks which right vertices have been considered in the CURRENT augmentation attempt, preventing infinite loops in the alternating path search.

common_mistakes: Not resetting the visited array before each DFS call — the visited array must be reset for each starting left vertex; reusing it across multiple augmentation attempts blocks valid paths

Using a global visited set instead of per-augmentation visited — the augmenting path DFS can revisit right vertices across different augmentation attempts (same right vertex could be part of different augmenting paths)
Confusing bipartite matching with perfect matching — maximum matching finds the most pairings possible; perfect matching requires every vertex to be paired (may not exist)
lessons.interview_relevance: Bipartite matching appears in assignment problems at companies with scheduling or allocation systems. The reduction to max flow connects bipartite matching to the broader max-flow framework. König's theorem (max matching = min vertex cover) is a theoretical result specifically tested at algorithm-focused companies. The O(VE) augmenting path algorithm is the expected solution.

flashcards.front: Bipartite matching: problem definition?
flashcards.back: Given a bipartite graph (two disjoint sets L and R, edges only between L and R), find the MAXIMUM MATCHING: the largest set of edges where no two edges share a vertex. Application: assign n workers to n tasks optimally.

flashcards.front: Augmenting path algorithm (Hopcroft-Karp / Hungarian): core idea?
flashcards.back: An augmenting path is a path from an unmatched left vertex to an unmatched right vertex, alternating between non-matching and matching edges. Adding the path to the matching (XOR) increases matching size by 1. Algorithm: find all augmenting paths repeatedly until none exist.

flashcards.front: König's theorem?
flashcards.back: In a bipartite graph: MAXIMUM MATCHING size = MINIMUM VERTEX COVER size. A vertex cover is a set of vertices that 'covers' every edge (at least one endpoint in the set). König's connects these two seemingly different problems. Not true for general graphs (where max matching ≤ min vertex cover).

flashcards.front: Maximum matching via DFS augmentation (simple O(VE) algorithm)?
flashcards.back: For each left vertex u: try to find an augmenting path via DFS. If a right vertex v is unmatched or its current match can find an alternative: augment. Repeat for all u. Total: O(V) left vertices × O(E) DFS each = O(VE). Hopcroft-Karp improves to O(E√V).

flashcards.front: Bipartite matching vs max flow relationship?
flashcards.back: Bipartite matching IS a max flow problem: add source→L vertices (capacity 1), L→R edges (capacity 1), R vertices→sink (capacity 1). Max flow = max matching. Ford-Fulkerson on this graph runs in O(VE) = O(matching augmentations × E).

flashcards.front: Independent set in bipartite graphs: by König's theorem?
flashcards.back: Maximum independent set = V - minimum vertex cover = V - maximum matching. An independent set is a set of vertices with no edges between them. König's theorem allows computing this efficiently for bipartite graphs (hard for general graphs — NP-complete).

quiz.question: Bipartite graph: L={1,2,3}, R={a,b,c}. Edges: 1-a, 1-b, 2-b, 3-c. Maximum matching size?
quiz.explanation: Matching: 1-a (or 1-b), 2-b, 3-c. If 1-b: then 2 can't use b → max matching = {1-b, 3-c} = size 2. If 1-a: then 2-b and 3-c → size 3. Maximum = 3. Greedy order matters; the augmenting path algorithm finds size 3.

quiz.question: König's theorem: max matching = 3 in a bipartite graph with 5 left + 5 right vertices. Min vertex cover size?
quiz.explanation: König's theorem: min vertex cover = max matching = 3. You need exactly 3 vertices to 'cover' all edges (each edge has at least one endpoint in the cover set).

quiz.question: Augmenting path: current matching = {1-a}. Edges available: 1-b, 2-a, 3-b. Is there an augmenting path starting from vertex 2?
options: No augmenting path from 2
Yes: 2→a (matched to 1)→1→b (unmatched) — augmenting path 2-a-1-b
Yes: 2→a directly (a is matched to 1, so skip)
Yes: 2→b directly
quiz.explanation: Augmenting path from unmatched left vertex 2: 2→a (a is matched to 1) →1 (follow matching edge backwards) →b (b is unmatched). Path: 2-a-1-b. Augment: flip edges. New matching: {2-a, 1-b}. Size 2.

quiz.question: Why does bipartite matching reduce to max flow?
options: Both use BFS
Adding a source/sink and capacity-1 edges converts the matching constraint into a flow capacity constraint — max flow through this network = max matching
Flow uses augmenting paths, matching uses DFS
No reduction — they are different problems
quiz.explanation: Flow network: source→each L vertex (capacity 1, ensures each L used ≤1 time). Each L→R edge (capacity 1). Each R vertex→sink (capacity 1, ensures each R used ≤1 time). Max flow through this network = max number of L-R edges usable subject to each vertex used at most once = max matching.

theory_mcq.question: In bipartite matching, an AUGMENTING PATH is 'alternating unmatched/matched edges from free to free vertex'. Why can we always IMPROVE matching by reversing an augmenting path?
options: Reversing an augmenting path maintains the same matching size

AN AUGMENTING PATH has these properties: starts at an UNMATCHED left vertex (free), ends at an UNMATCHED right vertex (free), alternates between unmatched→matched→unmatched edges; it has k+1 unmatched edges and k matched edges; REVERSING (swapping matched/unmatched along the path): the k+1 previously unmatched edges become matched, the k previously matched edges become unmatched; net change: +1 matched edge; every path vertex retains exactly one matched edge; augmenting paths always increase matching by exactly 1 — hence the name
Reversing an augmenting path only improves matching if all edges have equal weight
Augmenting paths can be reversed at most once per vertex
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's concept: 'Augmenting path: alternating unmatched/matched edges from free to free vertex' — an augmenting path has one more unmatched edge than matched; flipping matched/unmatched along the entire path increases matching by 1; the Berge's theorem: a matching is maximum iff no augmenting path exists; this is why we repeatedly search for augmenting paths until none exist.

theory_mcq.question: In the bipartite matching DFS, `matchR[v] === -1 || dfs(matchR[v], visited)` gives v to u even if v is already matched. Why is the recursive DFS call for the ALREADY-MATCHED vertex valid?
options: The recursion always returns false; it's a fallback path

ALTERNATING PATH SEARCH: if right vertex v is matched to left vertex m (matchR[v]=m), we try to RE-MATCH m to a DIFFERENT right vertex by calling dfs(m, visited); if m can find another right vertex, it moves there, freeing v for u; this is the 'augmenting path' search implemented recursively — v gives up its partner m, and m searches for a new partner; the `visited` array prevents exploring the same right vertex twice in one search, ensuring termination and correctness
The recursion is only entered when matchR[v] has unvisited neighbors
The recursive call finds a different left vertex to share with v
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's code: `if(matchR[v]===-1||dfs(matchR[v],visited))` — the recursive `dfs(matchR[v],visited)` searches for an augmenting path starting from the current partner of v; if it finds one, the current partner re-matches, freeing v for u; this implements alternating path search and is the core of the augmenting path algorithm.

logic_mcq.question: For 3 students and 3 jobs with edges [[0,0],[0,1],[1,1],[2,0],[2,2]], the maximum matching is 3. Trace the final matching.
options: Student 0→Job 1, Student 1→Job 1 (conflict!), Student 2→Job 0 — invalid
Student 0→Job 0 or 1, Student 1→Job 1, Student 2→Job 2 or 0; one valid perfect matching: matchL=[0,1,2] meaning 0→0, 1→1, 2→2 — confirmed by direct execution returning matching=3
Only 2 students can be matched; student 1 has only 1 option
Maximum matching is 2; student 2 must share job 0 with student 0
logic_mcq.explanation: Confirmed by direct execution: matching=3, matchL=[0,1,2]; the algorithm processes students 0,1,2 in order; student 0 takes job 0 (first available); student 1 takes job 1; student 2 tries job 0 (taken by 0), triggers re-matching: student 0 can also take job 1 — but that's taken by 1... student 0 takes job 1 then? Let me verify: matchL=[0,1,2] means 0→0,1→1,2→2 — student 2 directly gets job 2.

logic_mcq.question: Bipartite matching can be REDUCED to max flow. In this reduction, what capacity ensures at most one match per vertex?
options: Capacity 1 on all edges: source→left vertex (cap 1), bipartite edges (cap 1), right vertex→sink (cap 1); capacity 1 ensures each left vertex sends at most 1 unit of flow (one match) and each right vertex receives at most 1 unit (one match); max flow = max matching
Capacity = number of edges per vertex
Capacity ∞ on bipartite edges and 1 on source/sink edges
Capacity = degree of the vertex for adaptive matching
logic_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's concept: 'Reduction to max flow: add source/sink, all capacities 1' — each source→left edge has capacity 1, limiting each left vertex to one matched right vertex; each right→sink edge has capacity 1, limiting each right vertex to one matched left vertex; bipartite edges have capacity 1, providing the actual matching choices; max flow through this network equals maximum bipartite matching.

syntax_mcq.question: The bipartite matching DFS creates a NEW `visited` array for EACH left vertex u. Why not reuse a single visited array?
options: A single visited array would be faster and produce the same result

FRESH VISITED PER SEARCH: `visited[v]=true` marks right vertex v as 'already considered in the current augmenting path search'; this prevents infinite cycles when re-matching chains; if visited were shared across all left vertex searches, a right vertex marked visited during student 0's search would be skipped during student 1's search — missing valid augmenting paths; each new search for a left vertex starts from scratch, allowing it to explore all right vertices independently; the visited array is only for PREVENTING REVISITS WITHIN ONE DFS CALL, not across all calls
Creating a new array is mandatory because matchR is modified during DFS
The new array allows backtracking through previously visited vertices
syntax_mcq.explanation: Each augmenting path search from one left vertex is INDEPENDENT: visited prevents revisiting right vertices within the SAME search to avoid cycles; resetting visited for each left vertex allows a right vertex to be considered in multiple separate searches (for different left vertices); sharing visited across left vertex searches would incorrectly block valid paths that exist for later left vertices.

lessons.title: Max Flow — Ford-Fulkerson
lessons.objective: Implement Ford-Fulkerson max flow with BFS augmentation (Edmonds-Karp) in O(V*E²), understand the residual graph concept, and apply the max-flow min-cut theorem.
concepts: Max flow: maximum amount that can flow from source to sink in a capacity-constrained network
Residual graph: for each edge (u,v,cap), add reverse edge (v,u,0) for flow cancellation
Augmenting path: path from source to sink in residual graph with positive remaining capacity
Bottleneck capacity: minimum remaining capacity along the augmenting path
Ford-Fulkerson: find augmenting paths until none exist
Edmonds-Karp: use BFS for shortest augmenting path O(V*E^2)
Max-flow min-cut theorem: max flow = min cut capacity
Applications: network routing, bipartite matching, project selection
lessons.explanation: Max flow finds the maximum flow from a source s to a sink t in a directed graph with edge capacities. Ford-Fulkerson repeatedly finds augmenting paths (paths from s to t with remaining capacity) and sends flow along them. The residual graph tracks remaining capacity: for each edge (u,v) with capacity cap and current flow f, residual capacity is cap-f (forward) and f (backward, for flow cancellation). Edmonds-Karp uses BFS to find the shortest augmenting path, guaranteeing O(VE²) total time. Max-flow min-cut theorem: the maximum flow from s to t equals the minimum capacity of any cut (partition of vertices into S containing s and T containing t, with cut capacity = sum of capacities of edges from S to T). This duality connects network flow to graph partitioning. Applications: bipartite matching (add source/sink with capacity 1), project selection (which projects to undertake given dependencies), airline scheduling, and network capacity planning.
lessons.analogy: Max flow is like water flowing through pipes. Each pipe has a capacity (max water per second). You want to send as much water as possible from a source to a sink. If a pipe is full, you can 'cancel' flow by routing water back (residual backward edge). You keep finding new routes (augmenting paths) until no more water can reach the sink. The minimum cut is the bottleneck: the set of pipes that limits the total flow, and removing them disconnects source from sink.

code_example.explanation: The residual graph's backward edges are what make max flow powerful. Without backward edges, flow committed to a path cannot be 'undone' even if a better overall routing exists. The backward capacity (cap[v][u] += flow) allows future augmenting paths to route flow backward along previously committed paths, effectively rerouting the flow through better paths. This is how Ford-Fulkerson achieves the optimal maximum flow.

common_mistakes: Not adding backward edges in the residual graph — without backward edges, the algorithm cannot cancel previously committed flow; the backward capacity is what enables finding the true maximum flow

Using DFS instead of BFS for augmenting paths (using Ford-Fulkerson without Edmonds-Karp) — DFS may find long augmenting paths, giving O(E * max_flow) complexity which can be O(E * V * max_capacity); BFS guarantees O(VE²)
Not handling multiple edges between the same pair of vertices — if there are multiple edges from u to v with different capacities, sum them when initialising the capacity matrix
lessons.interview_relevance: Max flow appears in network capacity problems at infra-focused companies and in system design interviews about routing and load balancing. The max-flow min-cut theorem is specifically tested: 'What is the minimum cut in this network?' The reduction of bipartite matching to max flow demonstrates that these are instances of a general framework.

flashcards.front: Max Flow problem: definition?
flashcards.back: Given a directed graph with edge capacities, a source s, and a sink t: find the maximum amount of flow that can be sent from s to t, subject to: (1) capacity constraints (flow on each edge ≤ capacity), (2) conservation (flow in = flow out for every non-source/sink vertex).

flashcards.front: Ford-Fulkerson: core algorithm?
flashcards.back: While an augmenting path exists from s to t in the RESIDUAL GRAPH: find the path (DFS or BFS), compute bottleneck (min capacity on path), send that flow, update residual capacities. The residual graph has forward edges (remaining capacity) and backward edges (cancellation opportunity).

flashcards.front: Residual graph: what do backward edges enable?
flashcards.back: Backward edges (capacity = current flow on the forward edge) allow 'undoing' flow decisions. If we've sent 3 units on edge (u,v) with capacity 5: residual has (u,v) with capacity 2 (remaining forward) and (v,u) with capacity 3 (can cancel up to 3 units). This enables the algorithm to correct suboptimal earlier choices.

flashcards.front: Max-flow Min-cut theorem?
flashcards.back: Maximum flow value = minimum cut capacity. A cut partitions vertices into S (containing s) and T (containing t). Cut capacity = sum of capacities of edges from S to T. The theorem: the max flow that can be sent = the minimum over all cuts of the cut capacity.

flashcards.front: Ford-Fulkerson complexity: what determines it?
flashcards.back: O(E × max_flow) if using DFS (each augmentation takes O(E), max_flow augmentations needed). With BFS (Edmonds-Karp): O(V × E²) guaranteed — always augments along shortest paths, bounded number of augmentations. For integer capacities: Ford-Fulkerson terminates; for real capacities: may not terminate.

flashcards.front: Bipartite matching as max flow: capacity of each edge?
flashcards.back: Source→L: capacity 1 each. L→R edges: capacity 1 each. R→sink: capacity 1 each. Each unit of max flow corresponds to one matched pair. Ford-Fulkerson on this network runs in O(VE) since max flow ≤ min(|L|, |R|) augmentations, each taking O(V+E) BFS.

quiz.question: Flow network: s→a(cap=3), s→b(cap=2), a→t(cap=2), b→t(cap=3), a→b(cap=1). Max flow from s to t?
quiz.explanation: Two paths: s→a→t (capacity min(3,2)=2, send 2). s→b→t (capacity min(2,3)=2, send 2). Total = 4. Also s→a→b→t: min(3-2=1, 1, 3-2=1)=1, send 1 more. But after sending 2 on a→t, residual(a→t)=0. Try s→a→b→t: bottleneck=min(1,1,1)=1. Total = 2+2+... wait: s→a→b→t needs residual after first 2 paths. Max flow = 4.

quiz.question: Ford-Fulkerson: backward edges in residual allow?
options: Sending flow in the reverse direction unconditionally
Cancelling previously sent flow — equivalent to 'redirecting' flow via a different route
Adding more capacity to edges
Only DFS augmentation, not BFS
quiz.explanation: Backward edge (v→u with capacity = flow on u→v) represents: we can 'cancel' up to that much flow on u→v. This is equivalent to sending flow backward, or redirecting earlier flow decisions. It allows the algorithm to 'undo' suboptimal greedy choices.

quiz.question: Max-flow Min-cut: max flow = 4. There exists a cut where ALL edges from S to T have total capacity exactly?
options: 4 (the minimum cut capacity)
More than 4
Less than 4
Cannot determine
quiz.explanation: Max-flow Min-cut theorem: max flow = min cut capacity. If max flow = 4, the minimum cut has capacity exactly 4. There may be cuts with capacity > 4 (larger cuts), but the minimum is 4.

quiz.question: Edmonds-Karp (BFS augmentation) vs Ford-Fulkerson DFS: why is BFS guaranteed to terminate?
options: BFS processes edges in sorted order
BFS always finds the SHORTEST augmenting path — augmenting lengths are non-decreasing, and the total number of augmentations is bounded by O(VE)
BFS uses backward edges differently
BFS avoids cycles
quiz.explanation: Edmonds-Karp guarantees O(VE) augmentations because: (1) shortest augmenting path lengths are non-decreasing over augmentations, (2) each path length can increase at most V times, (3) at most E paths of each length → O(VE) total. Total runtime: O(VE × E) = O(VE²).

theory_mcq.question: In the max flow residual graph, why does adding a BACKWARD EDGE (reverse direction with 0 initial capacity) enable FLOW CANCELLATION?
options: Backward edges are just bookkeeping with no algorithmic effect

FLOW CANCELLATION via backward edges: when we push f units of flow along edge (u,v): forward capacity cap[u][v] decreases by f (less room); backward capacity cap[v][u] increases by f (f units CAN BE CANCELLED by pushing 'flow' backward); if a later augmenting path uses the backward edge (v,u): it 'cancels' f units of previously committed flow on (u,v), effectively rerouting that flow; this enables the algorithm to fix suboptimal early routing decisions without restarting; backward edges simulate the ability to 'undo' flow assignments during BFS exploration
Backward edges represent actual reverse flow in the physical network
Backward edges prevent paths from being counted twice in BFS
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's concept: 'Residual graph: for each edge (u,v,cap), add reverse edge (v,u,0) for flow cancellation' and the code: `cap[v][parent[v]] += flow` — the backward edge's capacity increases as flow goes forward; using the backward edge in a later BFS path effectively 'pulls back' previously committed flow, rerouting it through a better path.

theory_mcq.question: The MAX-FLOW MIN-CUT THEOREM states max flow = min cut capacity. What does this mean intuitively?
options: The maximum flow equals the number of edges in the minimum spanning tree

A CUT partitions vertices into {source side S} and {sink side T}; cut CAPACITY = sum of capacities of edges crossing S→T; the min cut is the partition with smallest total forward capacity; MAX FLOW = MIN CUT means: the BOTTLENECK that limits flow is exactly the minimum bottleneck partition of the graph; no flow exceeds min cut (flow must cross the cut); a flow equalling min cut is achievable; when Ford-Fulkerson terminates (no augmenting path), the BFS-reachable vertices form S, and the unreachable vertices form T — this natural partition is the min cut
Min cut = minimum number of edges to remove to disconnect source from sink
Max flow equals min cut only for unit-capacity networks
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's concept: 'Max-flow min-cut theorem: max flow = min cut capacity' — when no augmenting path exists, BFS from source reaches a set S (source side); all edges from S to T (sink side) are saturated (no residual capacity); the total capacity of these edges = the min cut = the max flow achieved.

logic_mcq.question: For the 6-node max flow example with edges [0→1(10), 0→2(10), 1→3(10), 2→4(10), 3→5(10), 4→5(10), 1→2(1)], the max flow is 20. Why?
options: Max flow = 20 because two independent paths each carry 10: path 0→1→3→5 (bottleneck 10) and path 0→2→4→5 (bottleneck 10); both paths are fully saturated; adding the edge 1→2 doesn't help further since both paths already carry maximum capacity
Max flow = 20 because the source has capacity 20 (two edges each 10)
Max flow is 21: the edge 1→2 allows one extra unit to flow
Max flow = 10; only one path can carry flow at a time
logic_mcq.explanation: Confirmed by direct execution: maxFlow=20; two disjoint paths: 0→1→3→5 with bottleneck min(10,10,10)=10 and 0→2→4→5 with bottleneck min(10,10,10)=10; total=20; the 1→2 edge (capacity 1) doesn't improve flow because both paths are already saturated; the source can send at most 10+10=20 units and the sink can receive at most 10+10=20 units.

logic_mcq.question: Edmonds-Karp uses BFS for augmenting paths. What advantage does BFS have over DFS for augmenting path selection?
options: BFS is used only for implementation simplicity; DFS produces identical performance

BFS FINDS SHORTEST AUGMENTING PATHS (fewest edges): Edmonds-Karp's O(VE²) bound relies on the guarantee that BFS finds shortest paths; using shortest paths ensures the total number of augmenting path iterations is bounded by O(VE) (each flow augmentation either saturates an edge or uses a longer path); DFS (basic Ford-Fulkerson) has no such bound — for integer capacities it's O(maxFlow) iterations, which can be O(V*maxCapacity) = exponential in the graph description size; BFS gives a polynomial-time guarantee
BFS uses less memory than DFS for large graphs
BFS always finds paths with maximum bottleneck capacity
logic_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's concept: 'Edmonds-Karp: use BFS for shortest augmenting path O(V*E^2)' — the shortest augmenting path guarantee is what converts Ford-Fulkerson from pseudo-polynomial O(maxFlow*E) to polynomial O(VE²); without BFS, adversarial graphs can make Ford-Fulkerson take an exponential number of iterations on irrational-capacity edges.

syntax_mcq.question: The max flow code uses `cap[u][v]` (adjacency MATRIX, not list). Why use a matrix for this implementation?
options: Adjacency matrix is always better for flow networks

RESIDUAL CAPACITY O(1) LOOKUP: the key operation is checking `cap[v][u] > 0` for ALL possible neighbors u in BFS; with adjacency matrix, `cap[v][u]` is O(1) regardless of whether edge (v,u) exists; with adjacency list, you'd need to maintain separate forward and backward edge objects and link them; for the backward edge update `cap[v][parent[v]] += flow`, the matrix allows O(1) updates without finding the specific backward edge object; for dense graphs (V small, many edges), the V² matrix overhead is acceptable; the tradeoff: O(V²) space and O(V) per BFS vertex vs O(E) space and O(degree) per BFS vertex with lists
Adjacency matrix is required because backward edges don't exist in the adjacency list
Matrix prevents overflow when flow values are large
syntax_mcq.explanation: The adjacency matrix simplifies the residual graph implementation: both forward capacity cap[u][v] and backward capacity cap[v][u] are stored at their natural positions; adding flow updates both O(1); BFS checks all V possible neighbors in O(V) per vertex; for max flow problems where V is small (competitive programming: V<=100-500), this O(V²) overhead is acceptable and simpler to code than adjacency list with paired edge objects.

lessons.title: Advanced Graph Thinking
lessons.objective: Select the correct advanced graph algorithm for any network or connectivity problem within 60 seconds, and map all Module 4 NeetCode 150 problems.
concepts: APSP: Floyd-Warshall O(V^3) or Dijkstra * V for sparse graphs
SCC: Tarjan's or Kosaraju's O(V+E), for strongly connected component analysis
Bridges/Articulation: DFS with low-link O(V+E), for network reliability
Bipartite matching: augmenting path O(VE) or Hopcroft-Karp O(E*sqrt(V))
Max flow: Edmonds-Karp O(VE^2), for capacity/routing problems
Min cut: equals max flow (max-flow min-cut theorem)
Module 4 NeetCode 150 problems mapped
Bridge to L3-M05: string algorithms use graph-like pattern matching
lessons.explanation: Advanced graph algorithms address four major problem categories beyond basic DFS/BFS and Dijkstra. APSP (All-Pairs Shortest Path): use Floyd-Warshall O(V³) for dense graphs or run Dijkstra V times O(V(V+E) log V) for sparse. Signal: 'find shortest path between all pairs', 'find the most connected city'. SCC (Strongly Connected Components): Tarjan's or Kosaraju's O(V+E). Signal: 'find cycles', 'identify strongly connected clusters', 'build condensation DAG'. Bridges and Articulation Points: DFS with low-links O(V+E). Signal: 'find critical connections', 'network reliability', 'single point of failure'. Bipartite Matching and Max Flow: augmenting path O(VE). Signal: 'assign tasks to workers', 'schedule jobs', 'route traffic through a network'. The max-flow min-cut duality connects these to graph partitioning problems. Senior engineers are expected to recognise these problem types from context clues (network reliability, capacity planning, assignment) and select the appropriate algorithm without prompting.
lessons.analogy: Advanced graph algorithm selection is like being a network engineer who diagnoses problems. SCC analysis is 'which parts of the network can communicate?'. Bridge finding is 'what single links would cause an outage?'. Max flow is 'how much traffic can we route?'. APSP is 'what are the fastest routes between all cities?'. Each question maps to a specific algorithm; the skill is the mapping, not the algorithm itself.

common_mistakes: Applying Floyd-Warshall to sparse graphs with large V — if V=10,000, Floyd-Warshall requires 10¹² = 10^12 operations; run Dijkstra V times instead (O(V*(V+E) log V) which is better for E << V²)

Using Tarjan's SCC algorithm on undirected graphs — in an undirected graph, every edge is a back edge making every component trivially strongly connected; use DFS for connected components in undirected graphs

Not recognising bipartite matching as a max-flow problem — this reduction enables solving matching problems with any max-flow implementation; knowing the connection avoids reimplementing matching from scratch
lessons.interview_relevance: Module 4 covers 2 NeetCode 150 problems (Find the City #1334, Critical Connections #1192). Both are hard graph problems. Bridges/articulation points are specifically mentioned in the module notes as appearing at 'infra-focused companies'. Max flow appears in system design DSA questions. The ability to recognise these problem types from real-world descriptions (network reliability, capacity planning) is the senior-level skill being evaluated.

(3) 'Find all clusters of microservices that are mutually dependent.' (4) 'Find the minimum latency between all pairs of edge nodes in a CDN.' Map each to its algorithm and state O(?) complexity.

flashcards.front: Advanced graph algorithm selection: 6-item decision tree?
flashcards.back: 1) All-pairs shortest paths → Floyd-Warshall O(V³). 2) Find strongly connected components → Tarjan's O(V+E). 3) Find bridges/articulation points → DFS with disc/low O(V+E). 4) Maximum bipartite matching → augmenting paths O(VE) or Hopcroft-Karp O(E√V). 5) Maximum flow → Edmonds-Karp O(VE²). 6) Minimum cut → max-flow then BFS in residual.

flashcards.front: SCC condensation: what problems does it unlock?
flashcards.back: After condensation to a DAG: topological sort (L3-M09), reachability queries (is u reachable from v?), 2-SAT (SAT with clauses of 2 literals → model as directed graph, SCC gives satisfying assignment), strongly connected graph augmentation (minimum edges to add to make graph strongly connected).

flashcards.front: 2-SAT: how does SCC solve it?
flashcards.back: Each variable x has two literals: x and ¬x. Each clause (a OR b) adds two directed edges: ¬a→b and ¬b→a. Build the implication graph. Run Tarjan's SCC. If x and ¬x are in the SAME SCC: unsatisfiable. Otherwise: set x=true if SCC(¬x) comes before SCC(x) in topological order.

flashcards.front: Min-cost max-flow: how does it extend max-flow?
flashcards.back: Each edge has a COST per unit of flow. Find max flow with minimum total cost. Algorithm: repeatedly find the minimum-cost augmenting path (via Bellman-Ford or SPFA instead of BFS). O(V × E × max_flow). Used in: optimal assignment, minimum cost bipartite matching, scheduling.

flashcards.front: Module 4 Level 3: industry relevance?
flashcards.back: Floyd-Warshall: used in routing protocols (OSPF), small network analysis. SCCs: compiler dependency analysis, web page ranking. Bridges/APs: network reliability analysis, finding single points of failure. Bipartite matching: scheduling, job assignment. Max flow: network capacity planning, image segmentation, project selection.

flashcards.front: Bridges vs cut edges in weighted graphs?
flashcards.back: Bridge = edge whose removal disconnects the graph. In weighted graphs, minimum cut (by capacity) ≠ minimum bridge (by weight). Max-flow/min-cut gives the minimum CAPACITY cut. Bridges are structural — they always disconnect; capacity of a bridge matters for flow problems.

quiz.question: Problem: 'Given a directed graph, find all pairs of vertices (u,v) where u is reachable from v.' Most efficient approach?
options: Floyd-Warshall O(V³) — direct computation
V × BFS/DFS O(V(V+E)) — from each vertex
Tarjan's SCC + condensation DAG + transitive closure O(V²+E)
Binary lifting O(V log V)
quiz.explanation: SCC condensation reduces the problem: vertices in the same SCC are mutually reachable. In the condensation DAG (at most V nodes, E edges), compute transitive closure. Total: O(V+E) SCC + O(V²) transitive closure. For dense graphs: O(V³) Floyd-Warshall may be comparable.

quiz.question: 2-SAT: clause (A OR B). Which directed edges are added to the implication graph?

¬A→B and ¬B→A
A→B and ¬A→B
¬A→¬B and ¬B→¬A
quiz.explanation: Clause (A OR B) = (¬A → B) AND (¬B → A). If A is false, B must be true. If B is false, A must be true. These are the two implication edges added.

theory_mcq.question: The lesson maps 4 algorithm types to signals. Which signal MOST CLEARLY distinguishes between Floyd-Warshall and single-source shortest path algorithms (Dijkstra/Bellman-Ford)?
options: Floyd-Warshall is chosen when there are negative edges

ALL-PAIRS vs SINGLE-SOURCE: Floyd-Warshall is for problems requiring SHORTEST PATHS BETWEEN EVERY PAIR of vertices ('find the city with fewest neighbors', 'connectivity between all pairs'); single-source algorithms (Dijkstra, Bellman-Ford) compute paths from ONE source; if the problem asks about all-pairs properties, Floyd-Warshall's O(V³) is natural; if only paths from one vertex are needed, running Floyd-Warshall is wasteful (Dijkstra is O(E log V) per source vs O(V²) per source for Floyd-Warshall in dense graphs)
Floyd-Warshall is chosen when the graph has fewer than 100 nodes
Floyd-Warshall is for undirected graphs; Dijkstra for directed
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's taxonomy: 'APSP: Floyd-Warshall O(V³)' vs single-source — the primary signal is whether ALL PAIRS of shortest paths are needed; Floyd-Warshall computes all n² pairs in O(n³); running Dijkstra from each source is O(VE log V) for sparse graphs (better than V³) but O(V³) for dense graphs (same asymptotically); the choice depends on graph density and whether all pairs are actually needed.

theory_mcq.question: Module 4 has 2 NC150 problems: #1334 (Find the City using Floyd-Warshall) and #1192 (Critical Connections using bridge finding). What is the COMMON PATTERN for recognising these?

#1334 SIGNAL: 'find city with fewest reachable neighbors within distance threshold' → ALL-PAIRS DISTANCE → Floyd-Warshall; #1192 SIGNAL: 'critical connections in a network' = 'which edges, if removed, disconnect the network' → BRIDGE FINDING → DFS with low-link values; the recognition pattern: (1) all-pairs reachability/distance → APSP; (2) single point/edge of failure → bridges/articulation points; these are the two 'connectivity analysis' algorithms in the module
Both use BFS with level tracking
Both are reducible to max flow
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's module4_problems: #1334 maps to Floyd-Warshall (all-pairs distance needed to count reachable cities per node) and #1192 maps to Bridge finding DFS (critical connections = bridges); the signal recognition: 'find city with fewest' implies comparing ALL pairs → APSP; 'critical connections' implies single-edge vulnerabilities → bridge DFS.

logic_mcq.question: Why is Bridges/Articulation Points restricted to UNDIRECTED graphs while Tarjan's SCC works on DIRECTED graphs?
options: The algorithms can be used for either graph type with minor modifications

CONCEPTUAL MISMATCH: Bridges/APs are defined for undirected graphs where 'connectivity' is symmetric (if u reaches v, v reaches u); an 'articulation point' in a directed graph is not well-defined (removing a vertex might disconnect some pairs but not others depending on direction); SCCs are naturally a directed concept (u and v are in the same SCC iff u→v and v→u); the disc/low algorithm for bridges uses the undirected 'skip parent' logic and counts undirected components; Tarjan's SCC uses directed DFS and onStack for directed path analysis
Bridges only work for undirected because low values can't be computed for directed graphs
Tarjan's SCC only works for directed because it uses a stack
logic_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's taxonomy: 'Bridges/Articulation: undirected graphs' vs 'Tarjan's SCC: directed graphs only' — bridges are defined on undirected graphs where an edge removal increases connected components; in directed graphs, 'connectivity' is asymmetric and SCCs capture the bidirectional reachability structure; the algorithms exploit the specific properties of their graph type.

logic_mcq.question: A company wants to assign 50 workers to 50 projects maximising the number of assignments (each worker can do multiple projects but only ONE project at a time). Which algorithm applies?
options: Maximum bipartite matching with leftCount=50 workers, rightCount=50 projects; edges represent worker-project compatibility; max matching = maximum number of simultaneous assignments
Floyd-Warshall to find the shortest assignment paths
Tarjan's SCC to find circular assignment dependencies
Max flow with unlimited capacity edges for each worker
logic_mcq.explanation: The problem is a classical BIPARTITE MATCHING: workers = left vertices, projects = right vertices, edges = valid assignments; maximum bipartite matching finds the maximum number of simultaneous assignments (each worker assigned to at most 1 project, each project to at most 1 worker); for 50×50 with up to 2500 edges, O(VE)=O(50*2500)=125,000 operations — trivially fast.

syntax_mcq.question: The `advancedGraphAlgorithms` array stores `signals` as STRING ARRAYS per algorithm. How does this design enable programmatic algorithm selection?
options: String arrays are required for display purposes only

PATTERN MATCHING LOOKUP: a function can check if a problem's description contains any signal keyword: `advancedGraphAlgorithms.find(a => a.signals.some(s => problemDesc.includes(s)))`; string arrays make each algorithm's trigger conditions explicit and testable; a single string per algorithm couldn't encode multiple independent signals ('all-pairs' OR 'most connected' OR 'dense graph' → Floyd-Warshall); array structure enables multi-keyword OR matching without complex parsing
Signal arrays are sorted alphabetically for binary search performance
String arrays prevent collisions between algorithm selection criteria
syntax_mcq.explanation: The signals array design enables: (1) multi-keyword trigger conditions per algorithm, (2) programmatic lookup via array methods like find/some, (3) extensibility (add new signals without changing the data structure); the alternative (a single description string) would require regex parsing; the array of strings is the natural representation for OR-conditions in a decision guide.

module_summary.difficulty: Hard — all algorithms require careful implementation; Tarjan's SCC, bridge/AP detection, and max flow are the most implementation-sensitive topics in competitive programming
core_patterns: Floyd-Warshall: k outer, i and j inner; dist[i][j]=min(dist[i][j], dist[i][k]+dist[k][j]); O(V³)
Floyd negative cycle: dist[i][i] < 0 after algorithm
Tarjan's SCC: disc[v]=low[v] → SCC root; pop stack; low update uses disc[u] ONLY if u is on stack
Bridge: low[child] > disc[parent] (strict >); AP: low[child] ≥ disc[parent] (≥)
Bridge/AP: skip parent when iterating neighbors in undirected DFS (avoid trivial back edge)
Bipartite matching: DFS augmenting path; O(VE) total; reduces to max flow with unit capacities
König's theorem: max matching = min vertex cover = V - max independent set (bipartite only)
Max flow residual: forward edge (remaining cap), backward edge (current flow = cancellable)
Edmonds-Karp: BFS finds shortest augmenting path; O(VE²) guaranteed termination
Min-cut: BFS from source in residual after max flow; S→T saturated edges = min cut

module_summary.key_implementation_insight: In ALL three DFS-based algorithms (Tarjan's SCC, bridges, articulation points), the critical distinction is: when a neighbor u is already visited, under what conditions do you use disc[u] vs low[u] to update low[v]? Tarjan's SCC: only if u is ON the DFS stack. Bridges/APs: only if u is NOT the direct parent. Getting these wrong produces completely wrong answers with no obvious symptoms.
